original_question: Non-equilibrium dynamics near a QCD critical point or a first-order phase transition can generate structures in moments of the net-baryon distribution, but do those fluctuation signals survive all the way to experimentally observable final-state quantities after the Cooper-Frye particlization step, the enforcement of conservation laws, additional Poisson sampling fluctuations, and subsequent hadronic rescattering?
target_in_paper: In Section 5 (“Non-equilibrium propagation of fluctuations”), page 6, lines 100–104: “In general, the non-equilibrium dynamics around a critical point or first order transition shows interesting features in moments of the net baryon distribution, but the question, if they survive to be observable still remains. Sticking to full dynamical approaches the Cooper–Frye transition poses challenges to the proper propagation of fluctuations. The enforcement of conservation laws will affect higher moments of conserved quantities and is usually not employed in sampling procedures. Also, the particle sampling on the hypersurface introduces Poisson fluctuations on top of the existing fluctuation signal. The hadronic rescattering further diminishes the amount of correlations that are observable in the final state by another 50 %.
correct_elements: The draft correctly identifies the open problem as the survival of non-equilibrium fluctuation signals in higher moments of the net-baryon distribution through the Cooper–Frye particlization, conservation-law enforcement, Poisson sampling, and hadronic rescattering.
missing_details: Specify that this question concerns heavy-ion collisions at intermediate beam energies in beam-energy scan experiments
Define precisely which moments (e.g. variance, skewness, kurtosis) of the net-baryon number are under consideration

State that the question refers to full dynamical simulations combining initial non-equilibrium evolution, fluctuating hydrodynamics around a QCD critical point or first-order transition, and subsequent particle transport
Clarify that Cooper–Frye particlization means hypersurface sampling of fluid cells into particles
Explain what is meant by enforcement of conservation laws (e.g. microcanonical constraints on energy, momentum, and baryon number during sampling)
Quantify the Poisson fluctuations introduced by hypersurface sampling as statistical noise added to fluctuation signals
Mention that hadronic rescattering in transport codes further reduces correlations by ~50 %
Define “survival to observable final-state quantities” as producing a measurable deviation in experimentally accessible cumulant observables
refined_question: In full dynamical simulations of relativistic heavy-ion collisions at intermediate beam energies that include a non-equilibrium passage through a QCD critical endpoint or a first-order phase transition with fluctuating hydrodynamics, do the enhancements in higher moments (variance, skewness, kurtosis) of the net-baryon number density survive (i) the Cooper–Frye hypersurface particlization with enforced global conservation of energy, momentum, and baryon number, (ii) the additional Poisson sampling fluctuations on the particlization surface, and (iii) the subsequent hadronic rescattering stage to yield a statistically significant deviation from baseline in final-state cumulant observables?
justification: The paper explicitly raises this open problem in Section 5 by stating that while non-equilibrium fluctuations around a critical point or first-order transition generate structures in the moments of the net-baryon distribution, it remains unknown whether these signals survive through Cooper–Frye sampling, conservation-law enforcement, Poisson noise, and hadronic rescattering to be experimentally observable. The draft captures the core components but omits definitions of the collision context, the specific moments, the nature of particlization and conservation enforcement, and what constitutes survival in terms of final observables. The refined question incorporates these details in a self-contained manner, matching the paper’s scope.
